extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, and patent prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed standards about when prosecution-history estoppel bars the doctrine of equivalents, drawn from Supreme Court argument in Festo v. SMC. Focuses on tests (foreseeability, presumptions/burdens, narrowing amendments), statutory alternatives (§112 sixth paragraph), and case law authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: IEEE foreseeability test
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding a patentability-based limiting amendment ... the doctrine of equivalents should be permitted to apply unless the limiting effect of the amended language with respect to an accused device would have been foreseeable at the time of the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IEEE recommended allowing equivalents except where the limiting effect would have been foreseeable to the applicant at the time of amendment. The brief states estoppel would be prohibited only where the objective inference from the patentee's language shows the equivalent subject matter was in fact abandoned during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed government presumptions and burdens before invoking equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. government's approach proposed various presumptions and burdens of proof before allowing the doctrine of equivalents to be invoked in the face of prosecution-history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice interest in the government's position centered on using presumptions/burdens as a check on equivalence; government characterized its test as backing off from a complete bar while still imposing evidentiary requirements on the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel applies where amendment 'surrenders' subject matter (narrowing to avoid prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel should apply only where the patent application disclaimed or 'surrendered' subject matter — i.e., amendments to avoid the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bork's position: no estoppel unless there was a 'surrender of subject matter'; he argued estoppel should be limited to amendments made to avoid prior art rejections. He opposed broader presumptions that would bar equivalents absent clear surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all claim amendments are 'narrowing' — estoppel depends on narrowing nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The real issue is whether an amendment was 'narrowing,' and not all amendments are narrowing amendments; estoppel arises from narrowing amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deputy Solicitor Wallace and others noted some Federal Circuit decisions find amendments not narrowing; section 112 (second paragraph) amendments can still be narrowing. Parties disputed how to define 'narrowing' and whether that term is workable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit Supply implied-disclaimer principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant narrows a claim, he gives up everything in between what was claimed and the prior art, and that this acts as an implied disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace repeatedly cited the 1942 Exhibit Supply case to support the proposition that narrowing amendments create an implied disclaimer and put the public on notice; this was used to justify estoppel against equivalents for narrowed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112 sixth paragraph (means-plus-function) as an alternative to doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 sixth paragraph provides a way for patent applicants to invoke equivalents without relying on the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neustadt argued applicants can draft claims in means-plus-function form to capture equivalents; this was presented as a statutory alternative and part of the argument that flexible-bar approaches are unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel from §112 second paragraph and enablement-related amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel could arise even where a claim was not amended to avoid the prior art (e.g., some §112, second paragraph amendments could be 'narrowing'); amendments made in response to enablement rejections should properly invoke estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties argued that amendments for reasons other than patentability (e.g., to address written-description/enablement problems) may nevertheless narrow the claim scope and produce estoppel implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of patentee to present evidence about what was surrendered
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where it is not clear what was surrendered, the patent owner should be entitled to present evidence regarding what was actually surrendered during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bork argued that when it's unclear what was given up, patentees must be able to introduce evidence to show the true scope surrendered; the Government and IEEE proposed presumptions but left room for evidentiary showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern about flexible-bar exception over-inclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: If exceptions to an absolute bar exist, everyone would try to fit into the exceptions, making a flexible bar unworkable or overly permissive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Souter and others worried that any flexible exceptions to a complete bar would be exploited; Neustadt countered that a flexible bar impedes innovation by creating uncertain 'gaps' for competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactivity and takings concerns from changing estoppel rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Festo decision's retroactive application could constitute a taking of property rights under the Constitution with retroactive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bork asserted the Federal Circuit rule had a retroactive takings effect on issued patents; the Court and counsel discussed whether changes in doctrine should be applied retroactively and the constitutional implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between literal infringement and equivalents in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent cases are decided on literal infringement, and courts must consider when doctrine of equivalents is needed as opposed to literal claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neustadt pointed to statistics (31 Federal Circuit cases favoring patent holder; most on literal infringement) to suggest doctrine of equivalents is not the predominant route; Justices asked how often equivalents are decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference vs. taking a contrary position as a basis for estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel may require drawing inferences from applicant behavior (such as amending claims) rather than proof of an explicit contrary position taken by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehnquist asked whether estoppel required a contrary position; Wallace argued reasonable inferences from behavior (amendments) can establish estoppel without an explicit contradictory statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claiming as a strategic patent-drafting choice to preserve equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may attempt to rely on means-plus-function claiming to achieve equivalents where the doctrine of equivalents might otherwise be limited by estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Breyer asked whether applicants could use §112 sixth paragraph claiming to preserve equivalents, indicating the interplay between claim-drafting technique and later infringement doctrines is a factor in evaluating patent scope.
